note.en: What you see: RUSH maps shock physiology in three parts remembered as pump, tank and pipes. Pump is the heart: contractility and pericardial fluid in the subxiphoid view. Tank is volume: the inferior vena cava for venous filling plus FAST windows and lung sliding for leaks into belly and chest. Pipes are the great vessels: the aorta for aneurysm or dissection and the leg veins for clot in suspected embolus. Together the three parts separate cardiogenic, hypovolaemic, obstructive and distributive shock at the bedside.

steps.en: What you see: RUSH maps shock physiology in three parts remembered as pump, tank and pipes. Pump is the heart: contractility and pericardial fluid in the subxiphoid view. Tank is volume: the inferior vena cava for venous filling plus FAST windows and lung sliding for leaks into belly and chest. Pipes are the great vessels: the aorta for aneurysm or dissection and the leg veins for clot in suspected embolus. Together the three parts separate cardiogenic, hypovolaemic, obstructive and distributive shock at the bedside.
Landmarks to confirm: Heart squeeze and pericardial space, inferior vena cava trunk, Morison pouch and splenorenal recess, bilateral pleural lines, abdominal aorta, femoral and popliteal veins.

Common mistakes and correction: Judging the pump from a foreshortened heart that overstates function: open the true apex before grading squeeze. Reading the cava without context in a ventilated patient: apply volume rules only with senior guidance. Skipping the pipes when the tank looks empty: a ruptured aneurysm hides outside the FAST windows.

Normal values with units: Pump: symmetric vigorous squeeze with no pericardial fluid. Tank: inferior vena cava 2.1 cm or less with collapse above 50 percent in a spontaneously breathing patient, no free fluid, bilateral sliding. Pipes: aorta without flap or focal ballooning, veins fully compressible. Any single abnormal part redirects resuscitation.

Pitfalls: Mixed shock is common in sepsis with cardiac disease, so do not force one label when two parts are abnormal. The protocol guides but never replaces pulse, pressure, lactate and clinical examination. In late pregnancy adjust windows for the uterus and involve obstetrics early.

todo.en: How to get it step by step: Run pump first: subxiphoid heart for squeeze and pericardial fluid. Then tank: inferior vena cava collapsibility, FAST belly windows and bilateral lung sliding. Then pipes: aorta in lengthwise plane and two point leg vein compression when embolus is suspected. State the emerging pattern after each part so the team can act early. Repeat the tank after each fluid challenge to track response.

q.en: What are the three parts of RUSH?

why.en: RUSH maps the heart as pump, volume as tank and great vessels as pipes.

q.en: What order does the protocol run?

o.en: Pump first, then tank, then pipes

why.en: Pump first catches tamponade and failure, then tank, then pipes.

q.en: Which pattern fits hypovolaemic shock with bleeding?

o.en: Flat collapsing cava with empty hyperdynamic heart and free fluid

why.en: An empty hyperdynamic heart with a flat cava and free fluid marks volume loss with a leak.

q.en: Pump and tank are both abnormal in sepsis with cardiac disease. What next?

o.en: Report both and treat both with senior guidance

why.en: Mixed shock is common, so report both patterns and treat both with senior guidance.
